title: Foundations of AI System Design
subtitle: Scope a machine learning system and design its data, features, models, deployment and monitoring, with a design document that catches data leakage before it ships.
outcomes: Turn a business problem into an ML problem statement with stakeholders, requirements, success metrics and a feasibility check
Design data collection, storage and versioning for an ML system, and handle missing data without leakage
Detect and fix target, preprocessing, temporal and group leakage in ML pipelines
Engineer, encode, scale and select features inside reproducible pipelines
Select, tune and evaluate models with validation that matches production and thresholds set by cost
Choose deployment and release strategies, and plan monitoring and retraining in a design document
prerequisites: Python and pandas basics, and supervised learning essentials: splitting data, fitting and scoring a scikit-learn model (Machine Learning Foundations with Python covers them; Data Analysis with Python and pandas helps). Install Python 3.10 or newer, then: pip install pandas scikit-learn duckdb joblib. The labs generate their own synthetic data.
description:
Most machine learning projects that fail in production don't fail because of the algorithm. They fail because the problem was framed loosely, the training data contained information the model would never see in real use, nobody decided how predictions would reach the people who act on them, or nobody noticed when the world changed. This course teaches the design work around the model: scoping a project with its stakeholders, requirements and success metrics; collecting, storing and versioning data; engineering features that exist at prediction time; selecting, tuning and evaluating models honestly; and deploying and monitoring them.

You'll work through one system end to end: a same-day delivery company that wants to warn customers before an order arrives late. You'll cost the trivial strategies and a rule baseline, build a versioned Parquet snapshot with DuckDB, catch three kinds of data leakage, compare models with time-aware cross-validation and set the warning threshold by cost, then package the model, batch-score a new week, run a shadow candidate and check for drift. Each lab adds sections to a design document, and the capstone asks you to design and prototype a new system, from ingestion to monitoring, on a fresh dataset with leaks of its own to find.

modules.title: Project Scoping and Requirements
modules.summary: Turn a vague request into a machine learning problem worth solving: the decision it supports, its stakeholders and requirements, how success is measured and whether it's feasible, written into the first sections of a design document.

lessons.title: From a business goal to an ML problem statement
objectives: Distinguish a business objective from the objective a model optimises
Frame a prediction task by its decision, target, unit and prediction time
Decide when a rule or heuristic is a better answer than machine learning
key_points: A business objective is the outcome an organisation wants, such as fewer late deliveries; an ML objective is what a model optimises, such as the probability that an order will be late. A design has to show how improving the second moves the first.

Frame every task precisely: the decision the prediction supports, the target, the unit of prediction (one row per order, customer or day), the moment the prediction is made, and the data that exists at that moment.

The decision sets the task type: classification for yes-or-no actions, regression for quantities, ranking when the output is an ordered list, and forecasting when the target is a future value of a time series.

Machine learning earns its cost when the pattern is too complex for hand-written rules, changes over time, and there is enough labelled data to learn it. When a simple rule meets the need, ship the rule.
Measure the current process or a simple heuristic first. That baseline is the bar a model must clear, and every later metric is reported against it.

lessons.title: Stakeholders, requirements and constraints
objectives: Identify the stakeholders of an ML system and what each needs from it
Write functional and non-functional requirements, including latency, throughput and freshness
Record constraints and conflicting needs as explicit decisions
key_points: Stakeholders include the people who act on predictions, the people affected by them, the owners of the data, the engineers who run the system, and legal, security and compliance reviewers. List what each needs and what each can block.
Functional requirements say what the system does, such as scoring every new order; non-functional requirements say how well: latency, throughput, availability, freshness of data and cost.

Latency and freshness decide the serving style early: a prediction needed while a customer waits calls for online serving, while predictions needed by tomorrow morning can come from a scheduled batch job.
Constraints come from data (what's collected and who owns it), law (privacy rules such as the GDPR), people (who labels and reviews) and operations (hardware, budget, cloud or on-premises).
Write conflicting needs down with the decision taken, such as accuracy against explainability or freshness against cost, so trade-offs aren't argued again every time the team changes.

lessons.title: Success metrics and feasibility
objectives: Define success with a business metric, an offline model metric and guardrail metrics
Assess feasibility: data at prediction time, labels, signal, cost and failure modes
key_points: Use three layers of metrics: a business metric (cost of late deliveries per week), an offline model metric that tracks it (recall at an acceptable precision), and guardrails that mustn't get worse (latency, complaint rate, fairness between groups).

Choose the model metric from the cost of each kind of error. When a missed positive costs far more than a false alarm, judge recall at a workable precision or expected cost, not accuracy, which looks high on imbalanced data.
Expected cost turns a confusion matrix into money or effort: multiply each outcome's count by its cost. Compare it with the trivial strategies, such as acting on every case or on none.

Feasibility asks four questions: do the inputs exist at prediction time, do labels exist or can they be collected, is there signal (does a quick baseline beat chance), and is the value worth building and running the system?
Plan for failure from the start: what happens when the model is wrong, slow, unavailable or out of date, and which fallback rule or human review takes over.

"""Write the course's synthetic delivery data: deliveries.csv (8 weeks of orders) and new_orders.csv (week 9).

The data is generated with a fixed seed (NumPy's RandomState, whose stream never changes between versions),
so everyone who runs this file gets exactly the same rows.  Run:  python make_deliveries.py
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ZONES = {"Z1": 2.5, "Z2": 3.5, "Z3": 4.5, "Z4": 5.5, "Z5": 6.5, "Z6": 8.0, "Z7": 9.5, "Z8": 11.0}


def make_orders(rng, start, days, n, drift=False):
    day = rng.randint(0, days, n)
    hour = rng.choice(np.arange(10, 23), n, p=np.array([4, 7, 10, 10, 6, 4, 4, 6, 10, 11, 9, 6, 13]) / 100)
    minute = rng.randint(0, 60, n)
    order_time = pd.Timestamp(start) + pd.to_timedelta(day, unit="D") + pd.to_timedelta(hour, unit="h") \
        + pd.to_timedelta(minute, unit="m")
    zone = rng.choice(list(ZONES), n, p=[0.16, 0.16, 0.14, 0.14, 0.12, 0.11, 0.09, 0.08])
    base = np.array([ZONES[z] for z in zone])
    if drift:                                   # week 9: a new suburb opens and orders travel further
        base = base * 1.35
    distance = np.round(np.clip(base * rng.lognormal(0, 0.35, n), 0.4, 25), 2)
    items = rng.randint(1, 13, n)
    rain_p = 0.45 if drift else 0.25
    day_weather = rng.choice(["clear", "rain", "storm"], days, p=[0.95 - rain_p, rain_p, 0.05])
    weather = day_weather[day]
    driver_num = rng.randint(1, 81, n)
    driver_id = np.array([f"D{d:03d}" for d in driver_num])
    skill = np.random.RandomState(7).normal(0, 4, 81)[driver_num]   # each driver's typical delay, in minutes
    new_driver = driver_num > 68                                     # 12 newest drivers have no rating yet
    rating = np.round(np.clip(4.6 - skill / 10 + rng.normal(0, 0.15, n), 3.0, 5.0), 1)
    rating = np.where(new_driver, np.nan, rating)
    promised = np.where(distance < 4, 30, np.where(distance < 9, 45, 60))
    rush = ((hour >= 12) & (hour <= 13)) | ((hour >= 18) & (hour <= 20))
    actual = (4 + distance * 3.4 + rush * 7 + (weather == "rain") * 6 + (weather == "storm") * 14
              + items * 0.6 + new_driver * 6 + skill + rng.normal(0, 7, n))
    actual = np.round(np.clip(actual, 6, None)).astype(int)
    late = (actual > promised).astype(int)
    complaint = (rng.rand(n) < np.where(late == 1, 0.45, 0.04)).astype(int)
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "order_time": order_time, "zone": zone, "distance_km": distance, "items": items, "weather": weather,
        "driver_id": driver_id, "driver_rating": rating, "promised_minutes": promised,
        "actual_minutes": actual, "customer_complaint": complaint, "late": late,
    }).sort_values("order_time", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
    return df


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
    orders = make_orders(rng, "2025-03-03", 56, 3000)
    orders.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(100001, 100001 + len(orders)))
    orders.to_csv("deliveries.csv", index=False)
    new = make_orders(rng, "2025-04-28", 7, 500, drift=True)
    new.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(200001, 200001 + len(new)))
    new.drop(columns=["actual_minutes", "customer_complaint", "late"]).to_csv("new_orders.csv", index=False)
    print(f"deliveries.csv: {len(orders)} orders from {orders.order_time.min():%Y-%m-%d} "
          f"to {orders.order_time.max():%Y-%m-%d}, {orders.late.mean():.1%} late")

modules.title: Data Engineering and Management
modules.summary: Plan where training data comes from and how it is labelled, stored, versioned and cleaned, so any model can be traced to the exact data it learnt from.

lessons.title: Collecting data and labels
objectives: Compare ways of collecting training data and labels
Log features at prediction time so they can be joined to outcomes later
Spot sampling bias and label quality problems early
key_points: Training data comes from logs of the current process, from instrumenting a product to record events, from manual labelling, from partners, or from synthetic data; each differs in cost, freshness and bias.

Labels are explicit (a person marks a ticket as urgent) or implicit, observed later from outcomes (an order arrived late). Implicit labels arrive with a delay, which sets how soon a model can be evaluated and retrained.

Log the features exactly as they were at prediction time, with a request or entity ID and a timestamp, so they can be joined to the outcome later. Rebuilding them afterwards from current tables quietly mixes in later values.
Sampling bias appears when the data doesn't represent the cases the model will meet: only cities already served, or only approved loans, because rejected applicants never show their outcome.
Check label quality before modelling: measure agreement between labellers on a sample, write labelling guidelines with examples, and store the guideline version with each label.

lessons.title: Storing data for ML: databases, warehouses, lakes and Parquet
objectives: Choose between operational databases, warehouses and data lakes for ML workloads
Explain why columnar formats such as Parquet suit training data
Use partitioning to keep large scans cheap
key_points: Operational (OLTP) databases serve an application one row at a time; analytical stores scan millions of rows and a few columns, which is how training sets are built. Train from an analytical copy, never by hammering the production database.

A data warehouse holds structured, modelled tables queried with SQL; a data lake holds files of any kind in cheap object storage; a lakehouse adds transactional table formats to the lake, combining the two.

Parquet stores data by column, with types, compression and per-column statistics, so a query that needs 3 of 50 columns reads only those 3, and files are usually several times smaller than the same data as CSV.

Partition big tables by a column most queries filter on, usually a date, so a job reading one week skips the other files. Thousands of tiny partitions slow everything down, so choose the grain with care.
DuckDB runs SQL in-process over CSV and Parquet files on a laptop, which makes it a practical way to prototype the queries that will later build training sets in a warehouse or lakehouse.

lessons.title: Versioning data and handling missing values
objectives: Version datasets so any model can be traced to the exact data it was trained on
Choose a strategy for missing values from their cause
Impute without leaking information from validation or test data
key_points: Data versioning means a model can name the exact data it learnt from: write immutable snapshots (new files, never edits), record a hash of the inputs and a checksum of the content, and keep a manifest with the model.
Hash the bytes of source files, but fingerprint Parquet snapshots by their content (row count and column sums), because writers of different versions produce different bytes for the same rows.
Tools such as DVC and lakeFS, and table formats with time travel such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg, version data at scale; the idea is the same as a hash in a manifest.

Missing values have causes: completely at random, related to another observed value, or related to the missing value itself, such as new drivers having no rating yet. The cause decides whether simple imputation is safe.

Options include dropping rows (only when few and random), imputing a statistic such as the median, imputing from other features, and adding a missing-indicator column so the model can learn from the fact that a value was absent.
Fit imputers on the training data only, then apply the same fitted imputer to validation, test and production data; computing the median over all the data leaks information from the test set.

modules.title: Advanced Feature Engineering
modules.summary: Build features that carry signal and exist at prediction time: extraction from raw records, leakage detection, categorical encodings, scaling and selection, all fitted inside pipelines.

lessons.title: Extracting features from raw data
objectives: Extract features from timestamps, transactions and text
Build time-window aggregates that use only past data
Explain training-serving skew and how shared feature code prevents it
key_points: Feature extraction turns raw records into numbers a model can use: parts of a date and time since an event from timestamps, counts and ratios from transactions, lengths and keyword flags from text.
Aggregates over a time window (orders in the last 7 days, average basket over 30 days) are often the strongest features, and each must be computed only from data before the prediction time.
Encode domain knowledge directly: a rush-hour flag lets a linear model capture a peak that a raw hour-of-day number can't, because the effect isn't a straight line in the hour.
Cyclical values such as hour of day or month can be encoded with sine and cosine so 23:00 and 00:00 end up close together; whether that helps depends on the shape of the real effect.
Training-serving skew happens when a feature is computed one way for training and another way in production. Define each feature once, in shared code or a feature store, and use it in both places.

lessons.title: Data leakage: how it happens and how to catch it
objectives: Name the main kinds of data leakage with an example of each
Detect leakage with an availability audit, a single-feature screen and a time-based split
key_points: Data leakage is information in training that won't exist when the model is used. It inflates offline scores, and the model then disappoints in production.
Target leakage: a feature recorded after, or because of, the outcome, such as the actual delivery minutes or a complaint flag when predicting lateness.

Preprocessing leakage: fitting scalers, imputers, encoders or feature selection on all the data before splitting lets test rows shape training. Put them in a Pipeline so each is fitted on training data only.
Temporal leakage: a random split of time-ordered data trains on the future. Split by time, and compute history features such as a driver's late rate only from earlier rows.
Group leakage: rows from the same customer or patient in both training and test let a model memorise individuals; split by entity, for example with GroupKFold.

Catch leaks with an availability audit (when is each column known?), a screen for single features with suspiciously high scores, and an honest time-based evaluation. A score that looks too good usually is.

lessons.title: Encoding categories and scaling numbers
objectives: Choose an encoding for low- and high-cardinality categorical features
Decide when scaling matters and which scaler to use
key_points: One-hot encoding makes a 0-or-1 column per category and suits a handful of categories; set handle_unknown="ignore" so a category first seen in production doesn't break the model.
Ordinal encoding suits categories with a real order (small, medium, large). For unordered categories it invents an order that a linear model will take literally.

High-cardinality categories, such as thousands of postcodes or product IDs, need another approach: group rare levels into "other", hash them into a fixed number of buckets, target-encode them, or learn an embedding.
Target encoding replaces a category with the average target for it, so it must be fitted out of fold; scikit-learn's TargetEncoder uses cross-fitting inside fit_transform for exactly this reason.

Standardisation (mean 0, standard deviation 1) matters for distance-based models, regularised linear models and neural networks; tree-based models split on thresholds and don't need it. RobustScaler resists outliers.

lessons.title: Selecting features
objectives: Compare filter, wrapper and embedded methods of feature selection
Use permutation importance on held-out data to judge a feature's value
key_points: Selecting features removes ones that add cost, noise or risk without adding signal: fewer features mean faster training and serving, fewer data dependencies and less to explain.

Filter methods score each feature on its own (correlation, mutual information); wrapper methods such as recursive feature elimination refit with subsets; embedded methods select while training, as L1 regularisation does.

Permutation importance measures how much a model's score drops when one feature's values are shuffled; computed on held-out data it works for any model and avoids the bias of impurity-based tree importances.
Selection is part of training: do it inside cross-validation, because choosing features with all the labels before splitting leaks the test set into the choice.
Every feature in production is a dependency to maintain. Prefer features whose source is reliable, available at prediction time and permitted for this use.

"""Write the course's synthetic delivery data: deliveries.csv (8 weeks of orders) and new_orders.csv (week 9).

The data is generated with a fixed seed (NumPy's RandomState, whose stream never changes between versions),
so everyone who runs this file gets exactly the same rows.  Run:  python make_deliveries.py
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ZONES = {"Z1": 2.5, "Z2": 3.5, "Z3": 4.5, "Z4": 5.5, "Z5": 6.5, "Z6": 8.0, "Z7": 9.5, "Z8": 11.0}


def make_orders(rng, start, days, n, drift=False):
    day = rng.randint(0, days, n)
    hour = rng.choice(np.arange(10, 23), n, p=np.array([4, 7, 10, 10, 6, 4, 4, 6, 10, 11, 9, 6, 13]) / 100)
    minute = rng.randint(0, 60, n)
    order_time = pd.Timestamp(start) + pd.to_timedelta(day, unit="D") + pd.to_timedelta(hour, unit="h") \
        + pd.to_timedelta(minute, unit="m")
    zone = rng.choice(list(ZONES), n, p=[0.16, 0.16, 0.14, 0.14, 0.12, 0.11, 0.09, 0.08])
    base = np.array([ZONES[z] for z in zone])
    if drift:                                   # week 9: a new suburb opens and orders travel further
        base = base * 1.35
    distance = np.round(np.clip(base * rng.lognormal(0, 0.35, n), 0.4, 25), 2)
    items = rng.randint(1, 13, n)
    rain_p = 0.45 if drift else 0.25
    day_weather = rng.choice(["clear", "rain", "storm"], days, p=[0.95 - rain_p, rain_p, 0.05])
    weather = day_weather[day]
    driver_num = rng.randint(1, 81, n)
    driver_id = np.array([f"D{d:03d}" for d in driver_num])
    skill = np.random.RandomState(7).normal(0, 4, 81)[driver_num]   # each driver's typical delay, in minutes
    new_driver = driver_num > 68                                     # 12 newest drivers have no rating yet
    rating = np.round(np.clip(4.6 - skill / 10 + rng.normal(0, 0.15, n), 3.0, 5.0), 1)
    rating = np.where(new_driver, np.nan, rating)
    promised = np.where(distance < 4, 30, np.where(distance < 9, 45, 60))
    rush = ((hour >= 12) & (hour <= 13)) | ((hour >= 18) & (hour <= 20))
    actual = (4 + distance * 3.4 + rush * 7 + (weather == "rain") * 6 + (weather == "storm") * 14
              + items * 0.6 + new_driver * 6 + skill + rng.normal(0, 7, n))
    actual = np.round(np.clip(actual, 6, None)).astype(int)
    late = (actual > promised).astype(int)
    complaint = (rng.rand(n) < np.where(late == 1, 0.45, 0.04)).astype(int)
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "order_time": order_time, "zone": zone, "distance_km": distance, "items": items, "weather": weather,
        "driver_id": driver_id, "driver_rating": rating, "promised_minutes": promised,
        "actual_minutes": actual, "customer_complaint": complaint, "late": late,
    }).sort_values("order_time", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
    return df


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
    orders = make_orders(rng, "2025-03-03", 56, 3000)
    orders.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(100001, 100001 + len(orders)))
    orders.to_csv("deliveries.csv", index=False)
    new = make_orders(rng, "2025-04-28", 7, 500, drift=True)
    new.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(200001, 200001 + len(new)))
    new.drop(columns=["actual_minutes", "customer_complaint", "late"]).to_csv("new_orders.csv", index=False)
    print(f"deliveries.csv: {len(orders)} orders from {orders.order_time.min():%Y-%m-%d} "
          f"to {orders.order_time.max():%Y-%m-%d}, {orders.late.mean():.1%} late")
    print(f"new_orders.csv: {len(new)} orders from {new.order_time.min():%Y-%m-%d} to {new.order_time.max():%Y-%m-%d}")

modules.title: Model Development and Evaluation
modules.summary: Choose candidate models, validate them the way they'll be used, tune them without fooling yourself, and judge them with metrics and thresholds that reflect what errors cost.

lessons.title: Choosing a model family
objectives: Compare model families for tabular, text and image problems
Weigh serving cost, interpretability and maintenance alongside the score
key_points: Start with a baseline and a simple model such as logistic or linear regression, then try stronger families. A more complex model has to beat the simple one by enough to justify its extra cost.

On tabular data, gradient-boosted trees (scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier, XGBoost, LightGBM) are usually strong; neural networks pay off mainly on images, audio, text and very large datasets.
A simple model can win: when the signal is mostly additive and the features are well engineered, a regularised linear model can match or beat boosted trees, and it is faster and easier to explain.
Selection weighs more than the score: prediction latency and memory, training cost, how much data the model needs, interpretability, and how easily it can be retrained and debugged.
Record each candidate's validation score, spread, training time and latency in the design document, so the choice is explained rather than just made.

lessons.title: Cross-validation that matches production
objectives: Explain k-fold, stratified, grouped and time-series cross-validation
Choose a validation scheme that copies how the model will be used
key_points: K-fold cross-validation trains k models, each validated on a different fold, and reports the mean and spread of their scores; the spread shows how far a single split's score can be trusted.
Stratified folds keep each class's share the same in every fold, which matters when one class is rare.
The split must copy production: TimeSeriesSplit always trains on earlier rows and validates on the next block; GroupKFold keeps every row of an entity, such as a customer, in a single fold.
Keep a final test set untouched and use it once. Choosing models or settings on it turns it into another validation set, and its score becomes optimistic.
Put all preprocessing in a Pipeline passed to cross_validate or a search, so each fold fits its own imputers, encoders and scalers.

lessons.title: Tuning hyperparameters
objectives: Distinguish hyperparameters from learnt parameters
Compare grid search, random search and adaptive search
Tune inside cross-validation and know when to stop
key_points: Hyperparameters are set before training (tree depth, learning rate, regularisation strength C); parameters are learnt from the data (coefficients, split thresholds).
Grid search tries every combination, so its cost multiplies with each hyperparameter; random search samples the space and usually finds good settings faster when only a few hyperparameters matter.
Adaptive methods spend more of the budget on promising settings: successive halving (HalvingGridSearchCV, still experimental in scikit-learn) and Bayesian optimisation tools such as Optuna.
Tune inside cross-validation on the training data only. Nested cross-validation, an outer loop around the whole search, estimates how well the tuning procedure itself generalises.
Fix random seeds, log every trial's settings and scores, and stop when improvements are smaller than the spread of the cross-validation scores.

lessons.title: Metrics and thresholds that match the decision
objectives: Choose classification and regression metrics for a decision
Pick a decision threshold from the costs of errors
Check calibration and per-segment performance
key_points: Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data: when 5% of cases are positive, predicting "no" every time scores 95%.

Precision is the share of predicted positives that are right; recall is the share of real positives found. The threshold trades one for the other, so choose it from the cost of each error on validation data, never on the test set.
ROC AUC measures how well the model ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds; average precision summarises the precision-recall curve and is more informative when positives are rare.

Calibration checks that predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Class weights and some models shift probabilities, which is fine for ranking but matters when probabilities feed costs; CalibratedClassifierCV can recalibrate them.

For regression, MAE is in the target's units, RMSE punishes large errors more, and MAPE breaks down near zero. Evaluate per segment too, because a good average can hide a group the model serves badly.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ZONES = {"Z1": 2.5, "Z2": 3.5, "Z3": 4.5, "Z4": 5.5, "Z5": 6.5, "Z6": 8.0, "Z7": 9.5, "Z8": 11.0}


def make_orders(rng, start, days, n, drift=False):
    day = rng.randint(0, days, n)
    hour = rng.choice(np.arange(10, 23), n, p=np.array([4, 7, 10, 10, 6, 4, 4, 6, 10, 11, 9, 6, 13]) / 100)
    minute = rng.randint(0, 60, n)
    order_time = pd.Timestamp(start) + pd.to_timedelta(day, unit="D") + pd.to_timedelta(hour, unit="h") \
        + pd.to_timedelta(minute, unit="m")
    zone = rng.choice(list(ZONES), n, p=[0.16, 0.16, 0.14, 0.14, 0.12, 0.11, 0.09, 0.08])
    base = np.array([ZONES[z] for z in zone])
    if drift:                                   # week 9: a new suburb opens and orders travel further
        base = base * 1.35
    distance = np.round(np.clip(base * rng.lognormal(0, 0.35, n), 0.4, 25), 2)
    items = rng.randint(1, 13, n)
    rain_p = 0.45 if drift else 0.25
    day_weather = rng.choice(["clear", "rain", "storm"], days, p=[0.95 - rain_p, rain_p, 0.05])
    weather = day_weather[day]
    driver_num = rng.randint(1, 81, n)
    driver_id = np.array([f"D{d:03d}" for d in driver_num])
    skill = np.random.RandomState(7).normal(0, 4, 81)[driver_num]   # each driver's typical delay, in minutes
    new_driver = driver_num > 68                                     # 12 newest drivers have no rating yet
    rating = np.round(np.clip(4.6 - skill / 10 + rng.normal(0, 0.15, n), 3.0, 5.0), 1)
    rating = np.where(new_driver, np.nan, rating)
    promised = np.where(distance < 4, 30, np.where(distance < 9, 45, 60))
    rush = ((hour >= 12) & (hour <= 13)) | ((hour >= 18) & (hour <= 20))
    actual = (4 + distance * 3.4 + rush * 7 + (weather == "rain") * 6 + (weather == "storm") * 14
              + items * 0.6 + new_driver * 6 + skill + rng.normal(0, 7, n))
    actual = np.round(np.clip(actual, 6, None)).astype(int)
    late = (actual > promised).astype(int)
    complaint = (rng.rand(n) < np.where(late == 1, 0.45, 0.04)).astype(int)
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "order_time": order_time, "zone": zone, "distance_km": distance, "items": items, "weather": weather,
        "driver_id": driver_id, "driver_rating": rating, "promised_minutes": promised,
        "actual_minutes": actual, "customer_complaint": complaint, "late": late,
    }).sort_values("order_time", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
    return df


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
    orders = make_orders(rng, "2025-03-03", 56, 3000)
    orders.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(100001, 100001 + len(orders)))
    orders.to_csv("deliveries.csv", index=False)
    new = make_orders(rng, "2025-04-28", 7, 500, drift=True)
    new.insert(0, "order_id", np.arange(200001, 200001 + len(new)))
    new.drop(columns=["actual_minutes", "customer_complaint", "late"]).to_csv("new_orders.csv", index=False)
    print(f"deliveries.csv: {len(orders)} orders from {orders.order_time.min():%Y-%m-%d} "
          f"to {orders.order_time.max():%Y-%m-%d}, {orders.late.mean():.1%} late")
    print(f"new_orders.csv: {len(new)} orders from {new.order_time.min():%Y-%m-%d} to {new.order_time.max():%Y-%m-%d}")

"""Lab 4: compare models with time-aware cross-validation, tune the best, pick a threshold by cost, test once."""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV, TimeSeriesSplit, cross_validate
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

SPLIT_DATE = "2025-04-14"
NUMERIC = ["distance_km", "items", "driver_rating", "promised_minutes", "hour", "rush_hour"]
CATEGORICAL = ["zone", "weather"]
WARN_COST, MISSED_COST = 2, 10


def load():
    df = pd.read_csv("deliveries.csv", parse_dates=["order_time"]).sort_values("order_time", kind="stable")
    df["hour"] = df["order_time"].dt.hour
    df["rush_hour"] = (df["hour"].between(12, 13) | df["hour"].between(18, 20)).astype(int)
    return df[df["order_time"] < SPLIT_DATE], df[df["order_time"] >= SPLIT_DATE]


def candidates():
    linear_prep = ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True), StandardScaler()), NUMERIC),
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), CATEGORICAL),
    ])
    tree_prep = ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", "passthrough", NUMERIC),        # histogram gradient boosting handles missing values itself
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False), CATEGORICAL),
    ])
    return {
        "baseline (prior)": make_pipeline(linear_prep, DummyClassifier(strategy="prior")),
        "logistic regression": make_pipeline(linear_prep, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
        "gradient boosting": make_pipeline(tree_prep, HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0)),
    }


def cost_per_1000(y, warned):
    y, warned = np.asarray(y), np.asarray(warned)
    return 1000 * (WARN_COST * warned.sum() + MISSED_COST * ((y == 1) & ~warned).sum()) / len(y)


def main():
    train, test = load()
    X, y = train[NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL], train["late"]
    cv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=4)               # always validate on weeks after the ones trained on
    print("Time-aware cross-validation (4 folds), ROC AUC:")
    # TODO: for each candidate, run cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc") and print
    #       the mean and standard deviation of result["test_score"]

    # TODO: tune the logistic regression with GridSearchCV over
    #       logisticregression__C in [0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0] and logisticregression__class_weight in [None, "balanced"],
    #       with cv=cv and scoring="roc_auc"; print the best settings and grid.best_score_
    grid = None

    search = RandomizedSearchCV(
        candidates()["gradient boosting"],
        {"histgradientboostingclassifier__learning_rate": [0.03, 0.05, 0.1],
         "histgradientboostingclassifier__max_depth": [2, 3, 4],
         "histgradientboostingclassifier__max_iter": [100, 200]},
        n_iter=6, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc", random_state=0)
    search.fit(X, y)
    print(f"Gradient boosting, best of 6 random settings: CV AUC {search.best_score_:.3f}")
    # TODO: once grid exists, keep whichever search scored higher
    chosen = search.best_estimator_
    print(f"Chosen: {chosen.steps[-1][0]}")

    # TODO: choose the threshold on out-of-fold predictions for the later folds, never on the test weeks:
    #       for each (tr, va) in cv.split(X), fit clone(chosen) on X.iloc[tr] and predict probabilities for X.iloc[va];
    #       then try thresholds np.arange(0.05, 0.95, 0.05) and keep the one with the lowest cost_per_1000
    threshold = 0.5
    print(f"Threshold chosen on validation folds: {threshold:.2f}")

    final = clone(chosen).fit(X, y)           # refit on all training weeks, then test once
    p_test = final.predict_proba(test[NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL])[:, 1]
    warned = p_test >= threshold
    tp = (warned & (test["late"] == 1)).sum()
    print(f"Test weeks 7-8: AUC {roc_auc_score(test['late'], p_test):.3f}  "
          f"average precision {average_precision_score(test['late'], p_test):.3f}")
    print(f"At {threshold:.2f}: precision {tp / warned.sum():.2f}  recall {tp / test['late'].sum():.2f}  "
          f"cost per 1,000 orders {cost_per_1000(test['late'], warned):.0f} "
          f"(warn everyone: {cost_per_1000(test['late'], np.ones(len(test), bool)):.0f})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")["test_score"] holds one score per fold.
Out-of-fold predictions only exist for the rows each fold validates on; start with proba = np.full(len(y), np.nan) and score only the rows that aren't NaN.
class_weight="balanced" pushes probabilities up for the rarer class, which is why the best threshold isn't 0.5: choose it on validation data, as here.

modules.title: Deployment and Monitoring
modules.summary: Choose how predictions reach the people and systems that use them, release new models safely, and plan the monitoring and retraining that keep a model useful.

lessons.title: Deployment strategies: batch, online and edge
objectives: Compare batch, online and edge prediction
Choose a strategy from freshness, volume, latency and connectivity requirements
key_points: Batch prediction scores many rows on a schedule and stores the results for lookup; it is simple and cheap, but predictions are only as fresh as the last run and new entities have none.
Online prediction scores each request when it arrives, behind an API; it handles new inputs and fresh features, at the cost of latency targets, scaling and someone on call.
Edge prediction runs the model on a phone, vehicle or machine: it works without a network and keeps data local, but limits the model's size and makes updates slower to roll out.
Choose by the requirements: how fresh predictions must be, how many there are, how quickly they are needed, and whether the inputs are known in advance.
Many systems mix them: precompute what can be precomputed in batch, and compute only request-time features and the final score online.

lessons.title: Serving a model and releasing it safely
objectives: Package a model so serving applies exactly the training-time transformations
Compare shadow, canary, blue-green and A/B releases
key_points: Package the whole pipeline, preprocessing and model, as one versioned artefact with its threshold and the facts about its training data, so serving can't apply different transformations.
A model service loads the artefact once at start-up, validates each request against a schema, and returns the prediction with the version of the model that made it.
A shadow deployment runs a new model on live traffic without acting on its answers, so it can be compared with the current one; a canary release then sends it a small share of real traffic first.

Blue-green deployment keeps the old version running beside the new one for instant rollback; an A/B test splits traffic at random to measure the effect on a business metric, with enough traffic to detect the difference that matters.
Always keep a fallback: the previous model, a cached prediction or a simple rule that answers when the model fails or times out.

lessons.title: Monitoring and retraining
objectives: Plan monitoring of the service, the data and the model
Measure distribution shift with the population stability index
Choose retraining triggers and a gate for new models
key_points: Monitor three levels: the service (latency, errors, throughput), the data (missing values, ranges, shifts in inputs and predictions) and the model (accuracy once labels arrive, and the business metric).

Data drift is a change in the inputs' distribution; concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and target. Labels often arrive late, so input and prediction drift are the early warnings.
The population stability index compares a live window with a reference, bin by bin. A common rule of thumb reads under 0.1 as stable, 0.1 to 0.25 as worth watching, and over 0.25 as a large shift.
Read the counts behind every alert: a category that vanishes for a week, such as no storms, makes the index jump, and seasonal swings can look like drift. Set thresholds from historical variation.
Retrain on a schedule, when a monitored metric crosses its threshold, or when enough new labels arrive; every retrained model must beat the current one on fresh data before it replaces it.

The data is generated with a fixed seed (NumPy's RandomState, whose stream never changes between versions),

    hour = rng.choice(np.arange(10, 23), n, p=np.array([4, 7, 10, 10, 6, 4, 4, 6, 10, 11, 9, 6, 13]) / 100)

    zone = rng.choice(list(ZONES), n, p=[0.16, 0.16, 0.14, 0.14, 0.12, 0.11, 0.09, 0.08])

    new_driver = driver_num > 68                                     # 12 newest drivers have no rating yet
    rating = np.round(np.clip(4.6 - skill / 10 + rng.normal(0, 0.15, n), 3.0, 5.0), 1)
    rating = np.where(new_driver, np.nan, rating)
    promised = np.where(distance < 4, 30, np.where(distance < 9, 45, 60))

"""Lab 5: package the model, batch-score week 9, compare a shadow candidate, and check for drift."""

from pathlib import Path

import duckdb
import joblib
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

NUMERIC = ["distance_km", "items", "driver_rating", "promised_minutes", "hour", "rush_hour"]
CATEGORICAL = ["zone", "weather"]
THRESHOLD = 0.40                 # chosen on validation folds in lab 4


def add_features(df):
    df = df.copy()
    df["hour"] = df["order_time"].dt.hour
    df["rush_hour"] = (df["hour"].between(12, 13) | df["hour"].between(18, 20)).astype(int)
    return df


def build(numeric):
    prep = ColumnTransformer([
        ("num", make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True), StandardScaler()), numeric),
        ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), CATEGORICAL),
    ])
    return make_pipeline(prep, LogisticRegression(C=10.0, class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000))


def package(train, version, numeric):
    pipeline = build(numeric).fit(train[numeric + CATEGORICAL], train["late"])
    bundle = {"version": version, "pipeline": pipeline, "threshold": THRESHOLD, "features": numeric + CATEGORICAL,
              "trained_on": {"rows": len(train), "from": str(train["order_time"].min().date()),
                             "to": str(train["order_time"].max().date())}}
    Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    joblib.dump(bundle, f"models/{version}.joblib")
    return bundle


def score(bundle, df):
    p = bundle["pipeline"].predict_proba(df[bundle["features"]])[:, 1]
    return pd.DataFrame({"order_id": df["order_id"], "p_late": p.round(4), "warn": p >= bundle["threshold"],
                         "model_version": bundle["version"]})


def psi(reference, live, bins=10):
    """Population stability index of a numeric column, with bins cut at the reference quantiles."""
    reference, live = pd.Series(reference).dropna(), pd.Series(live).dropna()
    # TODO: cut bins at the reference quantiles: edges = np.unique(np.quantile(reference, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)))
    #       and open the outer edges (edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf);
    #       share of reference and live values in each bin: np.histogram(values, edges)[0] / len(values);
    #       clip both shares at 1e-4 so empty bins don't divide by zero;
    #       return sum((live_share - ref_share) * ln(live_share / ref_share))
    return 0.0


def psi_categorical(reference, live):
    cats = sorted(set(reference) | set(live))
    ref = np.clip(pd.Series(reference).value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(cats, fill_value=0).to_numpy(), 1e-4, None)
    cur = np.clip(pd.Series(live).value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(cats, fill_value=0).to_numpy(), 1e-4, None)
    return float(np.sum((cur - ref) * np.log(cur / ref)))


def main():
    train = add_features(pd.read_csv("deliveries.csv", parse_dates=["order_time"]))
    week9 = add_features(pd.read_csv("new_orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_time"]))

    current = package(train, "late-v1", NUMERIC)
    candidate = package(train, "late-v2-candidate", [c for c in NUMERIC if c != "driver_rating"])
    print(f"Packaged {current['version']}: trained on {current['trained_on']}")

    # batch scoring: write the week's predictions where the dispatch app can look them up
    Path("predictions").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    scored = score(joblib.load("models/late-v1.joblib"), week9)
    # TODO: write scored to predictions/week_2025_18.parquet with DuckDB, which can query a pandas DataFrame
    #       by its variable name: duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM scored").write_parquet(...)
    # TODO: read the file back with DuckDB and print model_version, count(*) and the share warned:
    #       SELECT model_version, count(*) AS orders, round(avg(warn::INT), 3) AS share_warned
    #       FROM 'predictions/week_2025_18.parquet' GROUP BY model_version

    # shadow comparison: the candidate scores the same orders, but nobody acts on its answers
    shadow = score(candidate, week9)
    # TODO: the share of orders where the shadow's warn decision equals the current model's
    agree = 0.0
    print(f"Shadow {candidate['version']}: agrees on {agree:.1%} of orders, "
          f"warns {shadow['warn'].mean():.1%} vs {scored['warn'].mean():.1%}")

    # drift: compare week 9 with the training data, feature by feature, and the scores themselves
    print("Drift (PSI; under 0.1 stable, 0.1-0.25 watch, over 0.25 act):")
    report = {c: psi(train[c], week9[c]) for c in ["distance_km", "items", "driver_rating", "hour"]}
    report["weather"] = psi_categorical(train["weather"], week9["weather"])
    report["p_late (scores)"] = psi(score(current, train)["p_late"], scored["p_late"])
    for name, value in report.items():
        flag = "ACT" if value > 0.25 else "watch" if value > 0.1 else "ok"
        print(f"  {name:<16} {value:6.3f}  {flag}")
    if any(v > 0.25 for v in report.values()):
        print("Decision: open a retraining ticket and check week 9's lateness as soon as its labels arrive")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: np.histogram(values, edges)[0] counts the values in each bin; divide by len(values) to get shares.
PSI uses the reference's quantiles as bin edges, so each reference bin holds about a tenth of the training values.
The shadow's decisions are never sent to customers: only its agreement and its warn rate are logged.

project.title: Design and prototype an SLA-breach prediction system
project.brief: A software company's support team misses its resolution deadlines (SLAs) on about a third of tickets and wants to know, the moment a ticket is created, which ones are at risk, so a team lead can reassign or escalate them. make_tickets.py generates ten weeks of tickets with their outcomes (tickets.csv) and a new week without outcomes (new_tickets.csv); tickets_data_dictionary.csv says when each column becomes known. Design the system in a design document (all eleven sections of the template) and build a working prototype: ingest the CSV into a versioned Parquet snapshot with a manifest, audit the columns for leakage (several are known only after the ticket is answered or resolved), engineer features, compare at least three candidates with time-aware cross-validation, choose a threshold from costs you justify, test once on the last two weeks, batch-score the new week with a versioned artefact, and compute drift between the training data and the new week. Then recommend batch or online serving for this system, with a release and monitoring plan.
deliverables: A design document with all eleven sections completed, including a stakeholder table, three layers of metrics, a features table with known-at times, and a decision log
An ingestion script that writes a partitioned Parquet snapshot and a manifest with a source hash and a content checksum
A leakage audit naming each excluded column and the evidence (data dictionary, single-feature screen or honest evaluation)
A training script with time-aware cross-validation of at least three candidates, tuning, a cost-based threshold chosen on validation folds, and one final test

"""Write the capstone's synthetic support tickets: tickets.csv (10 weeks, with outcomes) and new_tickets.csv
(week 11, just created, no outcomes yet). Fixed seed: everyone gets the same rows.  Run: python make_tickets.py"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

SLA_HOURS = {"urgent": 4, "high": 8, "normal": 24, "low": 72}


def make(rng, start, days, n, week11=False):
    created = (pd.Timestamp(start) + pd.to_timedelta(rng.randint(0, days, n), unit="D")
               + pd.to_timedelta(rng.randint(7 * 60, 21 * 60, n), unit="m"))
    channel = rng.choice(["email", "chat", "phone", "web"], n, p=[0.35, 0.3, 0.15, 0.2])
    product = rng.choice(["billing", "app", "delivery", "account"], n, p=[0.3, 0.3, 0.25, 0.15])
    tier = rng.choice(["free", "plus", "business"], n, p=[0.55, 0.3, 0.15])
    priority = rng.choice(list(SLA_HOURS), n, p=[0.08, 0.22, 0.5, 0.2])
    length = np.round(rng.lognormal(5.3, 0.6, n)).astype(int)
    attachments = rng.poisson(0.6, n)
    queue = rng.poisson(28 if week11 else 18, n) + (created.dayofweek.to_numpy() == 0) * 10
    team = rng.choice(list("ABCDEF"), n)
    sla = np.array([SLA_HOURS[p] for p in priority])
    effort = (np.log1p(length) * 0.25 + attachments * 0.3 + (product == "billing") * 0.6
              + (channel == "email") * 0.5 - (tier == "business") * 0.4 + queue * 0.045
              + (team == "E") * 0.7 + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n))
    resolution_hours = np.round(np.exp(effort) * np.where(sla <= 8, 0.3, 1.0) + rng.exponential(1.0, n), 1)
    breached = (resolution_hours > sla).astype(int)
    first_response = np.round(np.clip(rng.gamma(2, 15 + queue * 1.5, n) * (1 + breached * 0.8), 1, None)).astype(int)
    csat = np.where(rng.rand(n) < 0.4, np.clip(np.round(4.3 - breached * 1.6 + rng.normal(0, 0.8, n)), 1, 5), np.nan)
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        "created_at": created, "channel": channel, "product": product, "customer_tier": tier,
        "priority": priority, "description_length": length, "attachments": attachments,
        "queue_size_at_creation": queue, "agent_team": team, "sla_hours": sla,
        "first_response_minutes": first_response,
        "resolved_at": created + pd.to_timedelta(resolution_hours, unit="h"),
        "csat_score": csat, "breached_sla": breached,
    }).sort_values("created_at", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
    df["resolved_at"] = df["resolved_at"].dt.floor("min")
    return df


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.RandomState(2025)
    tickets = make(rng, "2025-06-02", 70, 2400)
    tickets.insert(0, "ticket_id", [f"T{i:05d}" for i in range(1, len(tickets) + 1)])
    tickets.to_csv("tickets.csv", index=False)
    new = make(rng, "2025-08-11", 7, 300, week11=True)
    new.insert(0, "ticket_id", [f"T{i:05d}" for i in range(len(tickets) + 1, len(tickets) + len(new) + 1)])
    new.drop(columns=["first_response_minutes", "resolved_at", "csat_score", "breached_sla"]).to_csv(
        "new_tickets.csv", index=False)
    print(f"tickets.csv: {len(tickets)} tickets, {tickets.breached_sla.mean():.1%} breached their SLA")
    print(f"new_tickets.csv: {len(new)} tickets created {new.created_at.min():%Y-%m-%d} to {new.created_at.max():%Y-%m-%d}")
